lead: Two springs can sit one inside the other and share load. This concentric spring set packs high rate into small space and keeps working if one spring breaks. Railway buffers, clutch release mechanisms and valve trains use them. Fatigue matters: a spring in service is loaded millions of times, so wire must survive fluctuating shear stress, not just peak load. This chapter shows how load divides between nested springs, which clearances and solid heights to check, and how mean and alternating shear compare with a torsional endurance limit.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.5 for spring rate, Wahl factor and solid length, and Unit 2 for the S-N curve and Goodman line.

sections.h3: Nested springs share deflection, not load

blocks.text: Two helical compression springs of same free length can be nested, one inside other. They act in parallel: under total load W both compress by same δ.
P₁ = k₁δ,  P₂ = k₂δ,  W = P₁ + P₂ = (k₁ + k₂)δ
blocks.where: k₁ and k₂ are rates of outer and inner spring (N/mm); P₁ and P₂ are loads they carry (N); δ is common deflection (mm); W is total load (N).
k_total is rate of whole set (N/mm). Load splits in same ratio as rates, so stiffer spring carries bigger share.

items: High rate in small space: one 80 N/mm spring may not fit; 50 and 30 N/mm do.
Fail-safe action: if outer cracks, inner keeps carrying load at reduced rate.
Two-stage rate: if inner reaches solid height partway, further load goes to outer alone and rate drops to k₁.
Wound in opposite hands, outer right and inner left, so a broken coil cannot screw into the other and jam the set.

blocks.text: Inner spring must fit inside outer with radial gap about 1 mm or more each side. Touching coils rub, wear and lose coating.
Solid length L_s = N_t d, where N_t is total coils and d is wire diameter (mm). At solid height coils touch, deflection stops and rate jumps. Check each spring separately at maximum load.

items: Solid load P_s = k(L_f − L_s), with k its own rate and L_f free length (mm).
Require P₁ < P_s1 and P₂ < P_s2 with margin. Whichever goes solid first stops deflecting; the other takes further load.
Pass guide rod through inner spring to stop sideways buckling; rod must clear inner bore.

blocks.text: A spring in clutch or valve train sees load swinging between P_min and P_max, cycle after cycle. Fatigue cracks start inside coil, where shear stress is highest.

blocks.where: P_m is mean load and P_a alternating load, both in N; P_max and P_min are extreme loads of cycle, in N.
τ_m and τ_a are mean and alternating shear stress (MPa = N/mm²); K_w is Wahl factor (dimensionless); D is mean coil diameter and d wire diameter, both in mm.

blocks.text: Wahl factor multiplies both parts. Curvature and direct shear act at every instant, at mean load as well as peak, so K_w cannot apply to one only.

blocks.where: n is fatigue factor of safety; S_se is torsional endurance limit (MPa); S_su is torsional ultimate strength (MPa). Replace S_su by torsional yield strength S_sy for Soderberg line, which is more conservative.

items: S_su ≈ 0.67 S_ut and S_sy ≈ 0.45 S_ut, where S_ut is tensile ultimate strength of wire.
S_se ≈ 0.22 S_ut unpeened, ≈ 0.35 S_ut shot peened.
Shot peening leaves surface in compression, so surface crack must first overcome it and S_se rises.
Presetting (scragging) presses new spring to solid once. Residual stress lets it carry higher stress without permanent set.

blocks.text: These fractions are starting values for steel spring wire. Use endurance data of wire actually bought.

figure.caption: Load against deflection for the two nested springs of the worked example and for the set. At 150 mm the outer spring carries 7500 N, the inner 4500 N, and the pair carries 12 kN.

spec.aria: Load rises linearly with deflection for each spring; at 150 mm the outer carries 7500 N, the inner 4500 N, and the pair carries 12 kN.

examples.question: Two concentric helical compression springs have the same free length. The outer spring has rate k₁ = 50 N/mm and the inner spring k₂ = 30 N/mm. The set carries a total load W = 12 kN. (a) Find the common deflection. (b) Find the load in each spring. (c) The inner spring has a solid load of 5000 N. Does it clash at this deflection?
steps: Nested springs deflect together, so their rates add: k_total = k₁ + k₂ = 50 + 30 = 80 N/mm.
Convert the load: W = 12 kN = 12 000 N.
Outer spring load: P₁ = k₁δ = 50 × 150 = 7500 N.
Inner spring load: P₂ = k₂δ = 30 × 150 = 4500 N.
Check: P₁ + P₂ = 7500 + 4500 = 12 000 N, which matches W.
Clash check on the inner spring: P₂ = 4500 N against a solid load of 5000 N. Margin = 5000 − 4500 = 500 N, so the inner spring still has travel and does not go solid.
examples.answer: δ = 150 mm, the outer spring carries 7500 N and the inner 4500 N; the inner spring stays 500 N below its solid load.
examples.check:
k1 = 50
k2 = 30
W = 12000
kt = k1 + k2
d = W/kt
P1 = k1*d
P2 = k2*d
print(round(d, 2))
print(round(P1, 2))
print(round(P2, 2))
print(round(5000 - P2, 2))

examples.question: A helical compression spring is made of unpeened music wire with wire diameter d = 10 mm and mean coil diameter D = 80 mm. The tensile ultimate strength of the wire is S_ut = 1400 MPa. The working load fluctuates between P_min = 500 N and P_max = 1500 N. Find the Wahl factor, the mean and alternating shear stress, and the Goodman factor of safety.
steps: Mean load: P_m = (1500 + 500)/2 = 1000 N. Alternating load: P_a = (1500 − 500)/2 = 500 N.
Wire section factor: πd³ = π × 1000 = 3141.6 mm³.
Alternating shear stress: τ_a = K_w × 8P_aD/(πd³) = 1.184 × (8 × 500 × 80)/3141.6 = 120.6 MPa.
Material strengths: S_se = 0.22 S_ut = 0.22 × 1400 = 308 MPa; S_su = 0.67 S_ut = 0.67 × 1400 = 938 MPa.
examples.answer: K_w = 1.184, τ_m = 241.2 MPa, τ_a = 120.6 MPa, and the Goodman factor of safety is n ≈ 1.54.
examples.check:
from math import pi
d = 10.0
D = 80.0
Sut = 1400.0
Pmin = 500.0
Pmax = 1500.0
C = D/d
Kw = (4*C - 1)/(4*C - 4) + 0.615/C
Pm = (Pmax + Pmin)/2
Pa = (Pmax - Pmin)/2
tm = Kw*8*Pm*D/(pi*d**3)
ta = Kw*8*Pa*D/(pi*d**3)
Sse = 0.22*Sut
Ssu = 0.67*Sut
n = 1/(ta/Sse + tm/Ssu)
print(round(Kw, 3))
print(round(tm, 1))
print(round(ta, 1))
print(round(Sse, 0))
print(round(Ssu, 0))
print(round(n, 2))

traps: Halving total load between concentric springs. They share deflection, not load: P₁/P₂ = k₁/k₂, so stiffer spring carries more.
Adding deflections of nested springs. Nested springs share δ, so rates add. Deflections add only in series.
Applying Wahl factor to τ_m only or τ_a only. K_w multiplies both.
Comparing shear stress with tensile strength. Use S_se for τ_a and S_su (or S_sy for Soderberg) for τ_m.
Skipping clash check on inner spring. Smaller spring can go solid while outer still travels, changing rate.

quiz.q: Two concentric springs of the same free length have rates 40 N/mm and 25 N/mm. What is the rate of the set?
Why are the two springs of a nested set wound in opposite hands?
quiz.a: So that a broken coil of one spring cannot screw into the gap of the other and lock the set. The two springs then stay independent.

quiz.q: A nested set with k₁ = 45 N/mm and k₂ = 15 N/mm carries a total load of 6 kN. Find the common deflection and the load in each spring.
A spring has τ_m = 200 MPa and τ_a = 100 MPa. The wire gives S_se = 300 MPa and S_su = 900 MPa. Find the Goodman factor of safety.
An inner spring is designed to reach solid height at 60% of the full load of the set. Describe what happens to the set rate and to the load split beyond that point.
quiz.a: Up to 60% load both springs deflect together and the rate is k₁ + k₂. Once the inner spring is solid it cannot deflect further, so it holds a nearly constant load at its solid value and all extra load goes to the outer spring. The rate of the set falls to k₁ for further deflection.

quiz.q: Why does shot peening raise the fatigue limit of a spring?
quiz.a: It leaves the wire surface in residual compression. A fatigue crack starts at the surface in tension, so it must first overcome that compression; the torsional endurance limit rises, typically from about 0.22 S_ut to about 0.35 S_ut.

quiz.q: Two nested springs of equal rate carry equal stress, but only the outer one is shot peened. Which spring limits the fatigue life, and why?
quiz.a: The inner, unpeened spring. Its endurance limit is about 0.22 S_ut against about 0.35 S_ut for the peened outer spring, so at the same τ_a and τ_m the Goodman line gives it the lower factor of safety.

beyond: Not for the exam. Nested springs appear in engine valve trains, twin-rate suspension and safety valves, where a broken outer spring must not drop the load. Modern practice adds finite-element contact between coils and checks surge with fatigue, because a resonating coil can close its gap and spike the stress. Presetting and shot peening are separate process variables with their own data rather than fixed fractions of S_ut. Search 'spring fatigue Goodman shot peening', 'nested spring design clearance' and 'spring presetting scragging' to go further.
